idiom_name: public (non-open) entry point + open hooks at the module boundary
implementation_notes: Swift's access-control model expresses the split where library authors need it: a public (non-open) member can be called by clients of a framework but cannot be subclassed or overridden from outside the defining module, while open members are the deliberate extension points (the Swift book: open differs from public by allowing code outside the module to subclass and override). Write public func save() as the non-virtual interface and open func coreSave() as the hook; `final` closes a class or member completely. Inside the same module the compiler still allows overriding any visible member, so intra-module discipline is by convention - acceptable, because the guarantee that matters is against client code.
pitfalls: `open` and `public` are not interchangeable on the wrapper: open re-opens the contract for every importing module, public is the non-virtual half.

Extension points must be declared in the class body: methods added in extensions do not participate in dynamic dispatch the way class overrides do (and stored properties cannot be added in extensions at all).
A public class whose hooks are only public (not open) cannot be extended outside the module at all - if clients must subclass, both the class and the hooks need open.
